Issued at 112 PM EDT Tue Jul 21 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Northwest flow regime to carry through the forecast period, bringing 
quick moving disturbances, and variable short-term weather patterns 
across the Great Lakes region. Current upper air analysis showcases 
a closing surface low approaching James Bay that is currently in the 
process of dragging a cold frontal boundary across the region. 
Modest moisture pooling ahead of this front has allowed surface 
dewpoints to hold in the upper 50s to mid 60s. With ample lift with 
the onset of cold advection aloft in the wake of the front, coupled 
with diurnal heating to drum up instability, already festering 
convective responses are anticipated to increase in coverage across 
the region. Loss of daytime heating should put the kibosh on 
convection into the overnight hours, coupled with drier, cooler air 
streaming in from the northwest. Shortwave ridge intrudes by 
Wednesday, with large area of surface high pressure currently over 
the western Canadian Prairies moving in by Thursday. This will be 
quick to traverse the region, with backside return flow building by 
Friday. Resulting increase in moisture and heat will allow for 
instability to build back into the region by the weekend, carrying 
to early next week. In addition, additional subtle shortwave height 
disturbances will provide enough synoptic support to generate 
additional episodes of convection across the region Friday and 
beyond. 

Details: 

Today - Tomorrow: Cold front already advancing through the region, 
and has already commenced convective shower development across 
northern Michigan. Most of this activity set to produce minimal to 
no thunder... the lone exception being northeast lower south of M-
32. Axis of better instability progged to nose into this area, 
peaking around Saginaw Bay. While not exclusively outlooked, this 
area should be monitored for stronger discrete mode storms producing 
gusty winds and hail, owing to modest streamwise vorticity along 
with progged SBCAPE values ballooning up to 1500 J/kg. Limiting (not 
eliminating) the ceiling on convective potential is sub 30kt bulk 
shear, which may lead to a pulse-dominant mode to these storms... so 
if anything robust were to occur at the surface, it would be during 
the collapse of any updrafts. Anticipating diurnal instability to 
wane, and storm coverage to follow into the evening / overnight
as drier air surges in at the surface. 

Other story the next couple days will be the breezy WNW to NW winds. 
Sustained 10-20mph flow, gusting 35mph+ (strongest lakeshores) at 
times this afternoon... slackening a touch overnight before ramping 
back up sustained 10-15mph, gusts 30mph+ (again strongest 
lakeshores). Drier air at the surface and an intruding subsidence 
inversion should put a pretty big cap on shower activity into 
Wednesday... likely resulting in not much more than some autumnal 
feeling, poofy diurnal cumulus dominant day. Temps today today 
stonewall in the upper 60s to mid 70s for most, perhaps low 80s near 
Saginaw Bay. Overnight lows will respond well to the drier air 
moving in, despite winds limiting radiational cooling responses. 
Lows tonight in the upper 40s / low 50s inland, mid-upper 50s 
coasts. Highs Wednesday low-to-mid 60s eastern upper / west of I-75 
in northern lower, 70s elsewhere. Temps Wednesday night may make a 
run at 40 degrees flat in most cold spots, with mid 40s to near 50 
most other places... around 55 on the coasts. For those wondering if 
this is "windows open" sleeping weather regarding Canadian wildfire 
smoke... the answer should be yes. Latest modeled smoke trends are 
not robust over our area as recent rains across northwest Ontario 
and the Boundary Waters region of Minnesota have led to significant 
improvements in fire hot spots. Continued cooler weather in that 
region should keep things relatively under control the next few 
days, and conceptually should limit additional robust smoke plumes.

Rest of the Period: Seasonable air with temps in the upper 70s to 
lower 80s anticipated Thursday and beyond. High pressure keeps 
things dry and pleasant Thursday and Friday. Aforementioned return 
flow will bring more humid air into the region for the weekend, and 
with it, more chances for showers and thunderstorms. By no means 
does this pattern scream "washout", but certainly looks like chances 
for storms in the afternoon and evening hours Saturday through 
Monday. Overnight lows to creep a touch higher, possible settling 
into the upper 50s to mid 60s for a night or two. Not much of a 
signal for severe potential in this pattern, but it is important to 
note that NW flow dominant waves tend to have a high ceiling if 
everything can come together... but the chances of that actually 
happening are low for the time being.
